### Opportunities For Improvement

> O-2: The paper lacks comparative experiments with semi-supervised and other related method. One of the main contributions of the article is the introduction of the 'Species196-U' dataset, which consists of 1.2 million unlabeled data. However, the article does not provide direct evidence to demonstrate that these data can generate positive feedback based on the 'Species196-L' dataset in a fair experimental environment.

Thank you for your insightful suggestions. In response, we have expanded our experimental scope to include popular semi-supervised methods such as Mixmatch, FixMatch, and RemixMatch. In these experiments, we treated *Species196-L* as labeled data and *Species196-U* as unlabeled data. The results of these experiments using ResNet50 are shown below, indicating that our *Species196-U* dataset plays a role in these semi-supervised learning approaches:

| Models   | Method     | Top1 ACC(only Species-L) | Top1 ACC(semi-supervised using Specis-U) |
| :------- | :--------- | :----------------------: | :--------------------------------------: |
| Resnet50 | Mixmatch   |          64.32           |                  67.87                   |
| Resnet50 | Fixmatch   |          64.32           |                  66.94                   |
| Resnet50 | Remixmatch |          64.32           |                  69.30                   |

Additionally, we conducted experiments using contrastive learning methods such as Swav and MoCo v2. The linear probe results of *Species196-L* are as follows:

| Models   | Method  | Batch Size | Pretrain Data | Pretrain Epoch | Linear_cls Epoch | Top-1 ACC |
| :------- | :------ | :--------- | :------------ | :------------- | :--------------- | :-------- |
| Resnet50 | swav    | 256        | In1k          | 200            | 100              | 69.0      |
| Resnet50 | swav    | 256        | Species-U     | 200            | 100              | 69.7      |
| Resnet50 | MoCo v2 | 256        | In1k          | 800            | 100              | 67.1      |
| Resnet50 | MoCo v2 | 256        | Species-U     | 800            | 100              | 67.9      |

The results demonstrate that incorporating unlabeled data from *Species196-U* leads to a noticeable improvement in performance in both semi-supervised and contrastive learning settings.

Regarding your second point about the lack of direct evidence in our article to demonstrate the positive feedback generated by the *Species196-U* dataset based on the *Species196-L* dataset, we believe that we have addressed this in the *4.2.2 Masked image modeling* section of our paper, specifically in Table 5. The results of the Swin-B, Convnext-T, and Convnext-B models, when pretrained with *Species-U* using unsupervised masked image modeling, show a significant improvement compared to the results obtained with unsupervised pretraining using Imagenet-1K. Moreover, these improvements are achieved using the same scale of pretraining data, employing the same pretraining methods, and with the same number of epochs for both the pretraining and finetuning processes. So we think it's a fair experiment to show that *Species196-U* can generate positive feedback based on the *Species196-L* dataset.

> C-5: Did you visually verify the Species196-U, to ensure that the sampled images would match the intended class?

Thank you for your question. Even though the large volume of images in the Species196-U dataset makes manual verification of each image impractical, we have taken steps to visually inspect a subset of the data. To validate this, we conducted a visual inspection of images retrieved at various similarity ranks (100, 500, 1000, and 5000). This is illustrated in Appendix Figure 2 of our paper, where we present examples of these images. Even at a rank as high as 5000, the retrieved images still exhibit a substantial resemblance to the original species image, indicating a reasonable level of class consistency within the dataset.

Our approach to constructing the Species196-U dataset was designed with the understanding that not every sampled image would perfectly match the intended class. However, we aimed to ensure a level of visual similarity that would make the dataset valuable for semi-supervised and unsupervised learning scenarios.+

In summary, while we did not manually verify each image due to the dataset size, we did perform visual inspections to confirm that the Species196-U dataset contains images that are visually similar. We hope this addresses your question, and we appreciate your careful review of our work.

> C-6: In Line 182-183 it is stated that the dataset is like other fine grained dataset. Why not measure this using the method proposed in the paper "Measuring Dataset Granularity" by Cui et al.?

Thank you for your insightful comments and the suggestion to quantify the granularity of our dataset using the method proposed by Cui et al. in "Measuring Dataset Granularity".

We acknowledge the potential value of this method. However, at the time of our analysis, the implementation of this method was not publicly available, which made it impossible for us to directly apply their methodology to our dataset.

In response to your suggestion, we have utilized some related work mentioned in "Measuring Dataset Granularity" to evaluate our dataset. Specifically, we calculated several supervised and unsupervised metrics, including NMI, Rand Index, FMI, Silhouette score, Calinski-Harabasz score, and Davies-Bouldin score. These metrics were used to compare our *Species196-L* dataset with Cifar100 and Inat2021-mini-val). Features were extracted using a pretrained ResNet50 model from the PyTorch library, and clustering was performed using k-means.

The results are as follows:

| Metrics                 | Metrics Type | Cifar100  | Inat2021-mini | SPecies196-L |
| ----------------------- | ------------ | --------- | ------------- | ------------ |
| NMI                     | Supervised   | 0.06792   | 0.00185       | *0.00178* |
| Rand Index              | Supervised   | 0.00559   | -0.25609      | -*1.00513* |
| FMI                     | Supervised   | 0.01564   | 0.01209       | *0.01426*  |

| Davies-Bouldin score    | Unsupervised | 4.62351   | 4.54351        | *3.84286*  |

Thank you for your comment on our choice of performance metrics. We agree that the Top-1 accuracy may not fully capture the performance of a model on an imbalanced dataset.

In response to this feedback, we will supplement our main benchmark evaluation with macro F1 scores in the revised version of our paper. Macro F1 score (taking all classes as equally important) is a commonly used metric for multi-class classification problems, particularly when the classes are imbalanced.  

The F1 Score formula can be represented as:
$$
\text{F1 Score} = 2 \times \frac{{(\text{Precision} \times \text{Recall})}}{{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}}

The Macro F1 Score formula can be represented as:
$$
\text{Macro F1 Score} = \frac{{\text{F1 Score Class 1} + \text{F1 Score Class 2} + \ldots + \text{F1 Score Class N}}}{N}
$$

For the second part of your question, we conducted additional experiments under the same settings to compare the performance of Swin-B using SimMIM pretraining on both the iNat2021 dataset and our Species196-U dataset. We randomly sampled 1,200,000 images from the iNat2021 dataset for pretraining to ensure a fair comparison. The results are presented in the following table:

Thank you for your insightful question about the performance on rare classes and the challenges in data collection. For certain species, such as *Bruchidius incarnates* and *Schnaspis longirostris*, the available images for collection were indeed limited. These species aren't readily findable in biological databases like [iNaturalist ↗](https://www.inaturalist.org/) or [bugguide.net ↗](http://bugguide.net/), and the volume of accessible data on the internet is sparse.

This situation leads to an imbalance in our data. However, we view this as a reflection of the real-world distribution and availability of species data. Some species are simply more obscure and less documented than others. This presents a unique opportunity to develop models robust enough to handle such real-world imbalances and still deliver accurate results. We're continually working to refine our model to better handle such situations.

> O-7: The semi-supervised setup is unclear. Why do you not use the same backbone than your supervised experiment so that we can compare the approaches fairly ? The results are very weak compared to the supervised approach but it is hard to draw a conclusion.

1. **Diverse Objectives**: In the supervised learning section, our objective was to establish benchmarks. In the semi-supervised and self-supervised sections, we aimed to illustrate different methodologies' application to our dataset, *Species-U*.
2. **Resource Constraints**: The original Noisy Student setup is computationally intensive. It requires generating pseudo-labels for a vast number of unlabeled images from large-scale datasets such as JFT and YFCC100M, and involves an iterative training process where the student model matures into the teacher for subsequent iterations. Our dataset, *Species-U*, with only 1.2 million images, required a more streamlined approach, leading us to opt for smaller models.
In response to your feedback, we have conducted additional experiments. Supervised learning results of ResNet18 and ResNet34 will be included in Table 2.

### Limitations:

> L-1: Compared to fine-grained classification datasets (e.g., CUB-200-2011 and iNaturalist variants), the proposed dataset is large enough, but the class number is relatively small. During the data collection process, we aimed to maintain a sample size ranging between 50-200 for each category. However, for certain classes such as *IBruchidius incarnates* and *Schnaspis longirostris*, the number of available images was limited. This imbalance, we believe, mirrors the realities of the natural world where some categories are inherently more abundant or easier to capture than others. Rather than considering this as a limitation, we see it as a challenge for our dataset.

We understand that compared to fine-grained classification datasets like CUB-200-2011 and iNaturalist variants, our dataset has fewer classes. However, it's the real-world relevance and challenge that our dataset presents which we believe will be of interest and value to the research community. We look forward to seeing how researchers tackle these challenges to advance the state of the art in machine learning.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper proposes a new dataset of images of invasive species, and a fine-grained classification and detection benchmark. The dataset is divided into a small dataset of 19000 images with expert annotations, and a bigger dataset of 1.5M unlabelled images. The paper also proposes a comparison on the benchmark of different approaches, supervised, semi-supervised and self-supervised, using various backbones.

strengths.value:
- The proposed dataset is very useful in practice. It contains a lot of expert annotations of invasive species at a larger scale than previous work. It will be useful for both practitioners who want to specifically tackle this problem, and computer vision researchers who are looking for a fine-grained classification benchmark.

- The final comparison and analysis is extensive with many approaches (supervised, semi-supervised, self-supervised), backbones (convnets and vision transformers) and tasks (detection and classification).

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
- Could you give more details on the provenance of the images ? How many of them come from each dataset, how many of them are new.

- How do you ensure that the pictures are taken with a wide variety of poses and occlusion ? Do you think a model trained on your dataset would generalises to pictures taken in the wild with a phone or camera ?

- Could you give more specific details abut your comment L114-116 ? What does it mean to lower the difficulty in data acquisition ? Why do you think is has greater transfer potential ?

- It would be great to have an idea of the geographic repartition of the species present in your dataset, and more generally more info on the data so that it could be useful for practitioners at different locations on the planet.

- Do you check if roughly the data in Species196-U is in domain, and belongs to the 196 categories, or if there is a wide proportion of samples that belongs to other species, potentially none invasive ? With this information in mind, I would be curious to compare pretraining on Inat and pretraining on Species196-U for fine-tuning on Species196-L.

- How well do you do on rare classes ? Is it difficult to collect more data for these classes ? A deeper analysis would be interesting.

- The semi-supervised setup is unclear. Why do you not use the same backbone than your supervised experiment so that we can compare the approaches fairly ? The results are very weak compared to the supervised approach but it is hard to draw a conclusion.

- Have you tried to pretrain on both ImageNet and Species196-U and then fine-tune on Species196-L ?

documentation.value: The data collection process is described in details, although I would appreciate more details and statistics on the provenance of the images.

summary_and_contributions.value:
The paper proposes two new datasets, Species196-L and Species196-U, for classification of 196 invasive species. The  two datasets differ in how the data is collected and annotated. Species196-L contain 19K expert annotated images, whereas Species196-U contains 1.2 million images from the LAION-5B dataset, selected based on similarity to the classes of Species196-L but without labels.
The paper contains several benchmarks, comparing classification performance when training just on Species196-L, as well as pretraining with Species196-U. Object detection, as well as semi and self supervised benchmarks are also presented.

strengths.value: The paper presents a well crafted dataset, consisting of images with expert annotations of invasive species, accompanied with taxonomical information regarding the life stage of the pictured species. The combination with the large scale unlabeled Species196-U dataset, makes this a strong contribution to the fine-grained image analysis community, and very relevant. The datasets are thoroughly evaluated across several tasks.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: The dataset may be a bit small for modern purposes, as it only consists of 19K annotated images, compared to larger scale fine grained datasets such as Herbarium-19, PlantNet, and iNaturalist. There are also a set of considerations regarding the dataset assembly and benchmarks, see below.

limitations.value: There are not any immediate limitations of the presented work.

correctness.value:
The dataset construction and experiments are in general sound but there are some points to be addressed:

1) In line 146-147 it is stated that the dataset is split 1:1 into a training and test split. Why did you choose to not establish a validation split, in order to not overfit to the test split? This seems like a major oversight.
2) It is unclear how many of the images in the Species196-L dataset is bounding box annotated. Just a subset (L157-158) or all (L161-162)?
3) Why only use three images from Species196-L when sampling 8000 images per class for Species196-U? This seems like it would cause a large bias. 
4) It is unclear what is meant by the 120000 text-image pair remark in Line 180. Could you elaborate?
5) Did you visually verify the Species196-U, to ensure that the sampled images would match the intended class?
6) In Line 182-183 it is stated that the dataset is like other fine grained dataset. Why not measure this using the method proposed in the paper "Measuring Dataset Granularity" by Cui et al.?
7) It is unclear which type of accuracy is use in the benchmarks. Are you using the micro accuracy (i.e. average across all samples, favoring dominant classes) or macro accuracy (i.e. average per class accuracy, assigning equal weight to all classes)
8) It is unclear at which IoU threshold the object detection benchmark metrics are measured at.
9) It is unclear what kind, if any, hyperparameter searches was performed for the benchmarks.

clarity.value: The paper is written fairly well.

relation_to_prior_work.value: The paper positions itself well against the related works, and discuss many relevant previous works.

documentation.value: The paper documents the data collection process, availability and maintenance plans, and licensing.

1) Line 76-79, description of the deep learning's dependency on high quality annotated data.

summary_and_contributions.value: This article presents the creation of two datasets, Species196-L and Species196-U, for invasive species recognition. Species196-L focuses on insects, weeds, and mollusks and contains 19,236 images of 196 invasive species. The dataset includes a comprehensive taxonomy system and was collected from various online sources. Species196-U is a large-scale dataset obtained from LAION-5B using the clip-retrieval method, containing around 1.5 million unlabeled images of 196 insect and weed species. The challenges of the datasets include class similarity, low variability, and data imbalance. The article emphasizes the importance of accurate identification and location of invasive organisms for real-world applications.

strengths.value:
1.	The paper is generally easy to read and easy to follow.
2.	The paper states that bounding boxes were labeled for insect pests in accordance with the COCO format. This indicates that the dataset includes spatial information and enables sample-aware recognition, which can be beneficial for accurate pest location and categorization tasks.
3.	The establishment of a hierarchical taxonomy system, spanning from domain to species level, provides detailed classification information for each invasive species. This can be valuable for researchers and practitioners working in the field of invasive species identification and management.
4.	The Species196-L dataset includes images of invasive species at various life stages, such as eggs, larvae, pupae, and adults. This multi-grained approach allows for the study of different developmental stages and their impact on ecosystems and economies.
5.	The article provides a wealth of baseline experiments, offering significant assistance to other researchers in furthering this research endeavor.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1.	While the author has provided numerous baseline experimental results, they are limited to basic models. From a methodological perspective, the article lacks extensive experiments on fine-grained techniques, which are necessary for the continuation of this work. Based on the current provided experimental results, researchers could easily employ more powerful models to address the problem discussed in the paper, which is not expected.
2.	The paper lacks comparative experiments with semi-supervised and other related method. One of the main contributions of the article is the introduction of the 'Species196-U' dataset, which consists of 1.2 million unlabeled data. However, the article does not provide direct evidence to demonstrate that these data can generate positive feedback based on the 'Species196-L' dataset in a fair experimental environment.

limitations.value: I think authors have mentioned the limitations and potential negative societal impact of their work.

title.value: Species196: A One-Million Semi-supervised Dataset for Fine-grained Species Recognition

abstract.value: The development of foundation vision models has pushed the general visual recognition to a high level, but cannot well address the fine-grained recognition in specialized domain such as invasive species classification. Identifying and managing invasive species has strong social and ecological value. Currently, most invasive species datasets are limited in scale and cover a narrow range of species, which restricts the development of deep-learning based invasion biometrics systems. To fill the gap of this area, we introduced Species196, a large-scale semi-supervised dataset of 196-category invasive species. It collects over 19K images with expert-level accurate annotations (Species196-L), and 1.2M unlabeled images of invasive species (Species196-U). The dataset provides four experimental settings for benchmarking the existing models and algorithms, namely, supervised learning, semi-supervised learning and self-supervised pretraining. To facilitate future research on these four learning paradigms, we conduct an empirical study of the representative methods on the introduced dataset. The dataset will be made publicly available at https://species-dataset.github.io/.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
